questions.topic: An underdrawing read against the paint
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an underdrawing from the paint that covers it.
questions.stem: A margin note in the projection asks what separates an underdrawing from the paint that covers it. Which note is right?

options.text: The underdrawing is the first plan, and the paint may depart from it.
The underdrawing repeats the paint exactly, since painters never change course.
options.misconception: assumes the drawing and the paint can never differ

options.text: The underdrawing was made by a different workshop on a reused sheet.
options.misconception: assigns the drawing to a different hand without evidence

options.text: The underdrawing is a copy of a lost picture of the same region.
options.misconception: treats the drawing as a copy of another artwork

questions.explanation: The underdrawing is the plan laid down first, and the paint may depart from it as the work proceeds. A plan that never changed, a second workshop and a copy contradict the differences seen.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawing layer shows about the plan.

questions.topic: A radiograph read for an earlier composition
questions.learningObjective: State what reflectography contributes to a chart study.
questions.stem: The sheet legend records that infrared reflectography was carried out on a painted chart. What does that examination contribute?

options.text: The finished colours of the chart as they appear in daylight.
options.misconception: expects reflectography to show the finished colours

options.text: An earlier composition that the painter abandoned when he changed the coast.
The identity of the engraver who printed the chart in 1704.
options.misconception: reads an examination of the sheet as a record of printmakers

options.text: The date on which the chart was mounted on its wooden rollers.
options.misconception: treats an imaging examination as evidence about mounting

questions.explanation: Reflectography records the drawing beneath the paint, so it shows a composition the painter later abandoned. It does not show finished colours, identify an engraver or date the mounting.
questions.hint: Ask what layer the examination reaches.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An underdrawing read against the paint
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an underdrawing is read against the paint.
questions.stem: A graticule note asks why an underdrawing should be read against the paint rather than on its own.

answer.exemplar: An underdrawing records the plan the cartographer set out, while the painted chart records what he finally decided to show. Read together, the two show where the plan was kept, where it was abandoned and where it was corrected, and that sequence tells the reader how the work was made. Read alone, the drawing suggests a composition the finished sheet does not contain.

questions.explanation: The drawing and the paint are two stages of one work, so comparing them shows what was planned and what was kept. The underdrawing alone suggests a picture the finished chart does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison between layers reveals.

questions.stem: Another sheet note gives a weave of eighteen threads per centimetre in one area of a chart canvas and twenty-two in another. By how many threads per centimetre do the two areas differ?
questions.explanation: Twenty-two minus eighteen leaves a difference of four threads per centimetre. Averaging the two counts would give twenty and lose the difference that the weave records.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower count from the higher.

questions.learningObjective: State what a felling date establishes for a panel.

stimulus.body: A sheet annotation records a tree-ring report on a chart panel. The outermost plank gives a felling date of 1688 for the tree, and the paint is dated by other evidence to the 1720s.

questions.stem: The projection table records that a tree-ring report was made on a chart panel. What should the team record?

options.text: The tree-ring report is useless, since the plank was cut long before use.
options.misconception: dismisses the report without weighing what it still fixes

options.text: The chart was painted in 1688, because the tree was cut that year.
options.misconception: reads a felling date as the date the paint was applied

options.text: The panel's wood was felled in 1688, so the paint must postdate that date.
The paint and the wood agree, since both dates fall in the same decade.
options.misconception: claims agreement between dates that are decades apart

questions.explanation: A felling date fixes the earliest possible date for the wood and the work on it. It does not date the paint, which may be years later, and it is not useless if the plank was reused.
questions.hint: Ask what a felling date can and cannot fix.

questions.learningObjective: State what a lower limit of date establishes.
questions.stem: A scale bar note asks what physical evidence can establish and then to choose the option that fits.

options.text: The number of sheets in the atlas that the chart was later bound with.
options.misconception: treats dating evidence as proof of later binding history

options.text: The exact year the chart was signed and coloured in the workshop.
options.misconception: treats an earliest date as the exact year of making

options.text: The identity of the hydrographer who collected the soundings shown.
options.misconception: claims material evidence can identify who surveyed the coast

options.text: An earliest possible date for the object, not the date it was finished.

questions.explanation: This kind of evidence fixes a lower bound, so it says the object cannot be earlier than a certain point. The finished date, the surveyor's name and the binding history need separate evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the date is a floor or a ceiling.

options.text: As a tracing of a finished chart by a later hand in the same workshop.
options.misconception: treats the underdrawing as a tracing made after the chart

options.text: As a plan that the painter was free to keep or abandon while working.
As a decoration prepared for a different sheet and later cut up.
options.misconception: assumes the drawing was made for another object

options.text: As a repair record in which the paint was added over the drawing.
options.misconception: confuses the drawing layer with later restoration work

questions.explanation: The drawing is the first working state, and the paint records the decisions taken afterwards. A later tracing, a decoration for another sheet or a repair record misreads its place in the layers.
questions.hint: Ask which stage of the work the drawing is.

questions.stem: The sheet index describes an X-radiograph of a chart panel showing a nail and a horizontal join. What does it establish?

options.text: That the panel has never been lined or cradled by a later restorer.
options.misconception: reads the absence of one sign as proof of no later work

options.text: That the chart was painted by the workshop that made the join.
options.misconception: turns a construction detail into evidence of a workshop

options.text: That the panel was made from joined boards fitted with metal fastenings.
That the chart is older than the atlas in which it now appears.
options.misconception: turns a construction detail into a claim about the atlas

questions.explanation: A radiograph shows density, so a nail and a join demonstrate that the panel is built from fitted boards. It does not identify a workshop, prove that no later lining occurred, or date the atlas.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pigment analysis as a dating constraint
questions.learningObjective: Explain how pigment analysis constrains a date.
questions.stem: A projection room note asks how a pigment analysis should be turned into a dating constraint for a chart.

answer.exemplar: Pigment analysis identifies what the paint contains, and some pigments only began to be manufactured at a known date. A chart that uses such a pigment cannot have been painted before that date, which gives the work a terminus post quem: a floor below which it cannot fall. The constraint does not date the chart, because a painter may keep an old pigment on the shelf or a workshop may hold old stock for years.

questions.explanation: A pigment that only came into use at a known date sets a floor below which the work cannot fall. It never gives the date itself, since old pigment can be kept and reused for years afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what the pigment rules out and what it cannot give.

questions.stem: The gazetteer note lists nine pieces of evidence for the chart's date and rules out six of them. How many of the nine pieces remain possible?
questions.explanation: Nine pieces of evidence minus the six ruled out leaves three that remain possible, since nine minus six equals three. Treating a ruled-out piece as possible would give four.
questions.hint: Subtract the ruled-out pieces from the total.

questions.topic: Pigment analysis as a dating constraint

questions.stem: A sheet annotation compares two dated reports of the harbour wall. What does the pigment result rule out?

options.text: It disproves the pigment result, since engravings predate manufactured colour.
options.misconception: dismisses a laboratory result without contrary evidence

options.text: It fixes the chart as a work of 1812 or later.
options.misconception: treats the earliest date as though it were the finished date

options.text: It shows the blue was added later, as a nineteenth century overpaint.
options.misconception: invents a later overpaint to reconcile the two dates

options.text: It rules out the chart having been painted with this blue before 1812.

questions.explanation: A pigment that only existed from 1812 cannot appear in paint applied earlier, so the two dates cannot both stand for the same painting. The result does not make 1812 the date of the work.
questions.hint: Ask which date the pigment rules out.

options.text: That the chart was painted by the weaver's family in the same town.
options.misconception: turns a weaving method into a claim about the painter

options.text: That the canvas was woven in a particular way, and where it was probably made.
That the chart is a copy made after the original was lost.
options.misconception: reads the weave as evidence of a later copy

options.text: That the chart was painted at sea, on a vessel with its own canvas.
options.misconception: treats a canvas weave as evidence of the place of painting

questions.explanation: A weave sample describes how the canvas was made, and characteristic patterns can point to a place of manufacture. It does not name a painter, prove a copy, or locate the painting.

options.text: The name of the colourman who ground and sold the pigment.
options.misconception: assumes pigment analysis names the supplier of the colour

options.text: The exact year of the chart, since each pigment was made in one year.
options.misconception: assumes a pigment carries the exact year of the chart

A ranking of the chart among other sheets painted in the same period.
options.misconception: treats a dating constraint as a ranking of quality

questions.explanation: A pigment with a known first manufacture date sets a floor for the work, and that is what the analysis gives. It never yields the finished year, the supplier's name or a place in a ranking of sheets.

questions.stem: A second set of findings is compared on the sheet with the dates proposed. Which reading is right?

options.text: The ring date proves the chart is a copy of an earlier original.
options.misconception: turns a dating floor into a claim about copying

options.text: The ring date proves the chart was painted in the year the tree fell.

options.misconception: dismisses the ring date as meaningless for reused timber

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A radiograph read for an earlier composition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a radiograph is read for an earlier state.
questions.stem: Two survey notes are asked to explain why a radiograph is read for an earlier composition rather than for the finished chart.

answer.exemplar: A radiograph compares how much X-rays are absorbed by the material, so lead white, metal fastenings, changes of ground and alterations to the support all appear in it as differences of density. Where the painter abandoned a first arrangement, the removal and replacement of material often leave a trace, and that trace can be read as the shape of the earlier composition, even where no drawing survives.

questions.explanation: The radiograph records differences in density, and altered material leaves traces of the earlier arrangement. It is read for that earlier state, since the finished sheet is visible.
questions.hint: Ask what an altered layer leaves behind.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a terminus post quem does
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a radiograph cannot settle a date.
questions.stem: The survey team is asked to explain why a radiograph cannot settle the date of a chart, and to explain.

answer.exemplar: A radiograph records differences in density, and among the things it can show are changes of ground, metal fastenings, replaced areas and alterations to the support. All of these bear on how the chart was made and, sometimes, on how high it dates, but none of them is a clock. A date has to come from a dated fact of some kind, such as a pigment with a known origin, a written record or a felling date from the wood.

questions.explanation: A radiograph shows density, and density tells about construction rather than about years. A date must come from a dated fact such as a pigment's origin, a written record or a felling date.
questions.hint: Ask whether the image gives a number of years.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a terminus post quem does
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a dating constraint should be presented.
questions.stem: The sheet editors are asked how a dating constraint should be worded in a printed catalogue.

answer.exemplar: The catalogue should state the constraint as a limit rather than as a date, saying that the paint contains a pigment not available before a given year, so the sheet cannot be earlier than that. Readers can then weigh the constraint against the other evidence, and a later catalogue note can show whether the constraint has been tightened by further analysis.

questions.explanation: A constraint should be presented as a floor on possibility, so that readers can weigh it against other evidence. Printing it as a finished date would claim more than the analysis can carry.
questions.hint: Ask how a limit should be worded in a catalogue.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A panel made from older boards
questions.learningObjective: Explain what reused boards mean for dating.
questions.stem: The projection team is asked what a panel made from older boards means for dating a chart.

answer.exemplar: Boards cut for one purpose and used for another carry their earlier history into the later work. The felling date of the timber therefore sets a limit: whatever else is known, the chart cannot be earlier than the wood. At the same time the interval between cutting and painting can be long, and a panel may be reused decades afterwards, so the wood constrains the date without fixing it.

questions.explanation: Reused boards set a floor for the work and may widen the gap between the wood and the painting. They constrain the date without fixing it, since the interval between cutting and use can be long.
questions.hint: Ask what the wood can still fix.

questions.explanation: Four of the seven boards carry earlier nail holes, so the fraction is four divided by seven, which is about 0.57. Counting all seven boards as reused would ignore the three with no holes at all.
questions.hint: Divide the marked boards by the total number of boards.

options.misconception: confuses an altered area with a later lining canvas

questions.explanation: The paler rectangle and the continuing pen lines show an earlier shoreline that was painted over. A second sheet, a printing fault and a later lining each misread what the density difference shows.

questions.learningObjective: Define what a terminus post quem rules out.
questions.stem: Another annotation asks what a terminus post quem does and then to choose the option that fits.

options.text: It gives the year the work was signed, dated and sent to the printer.
options.misconception: treats a floor as though it were the finished date

options.text: It fixes the latest date possible for the work, ruling out later ones.
options.misconception: reverses the sense of a terminus post quem into a limit

options.text: It fixes the earliest date possible for the work, ruling out earlier ones.
It shows that the work was made in the year of the earliest record.
options.misconception: assumes the earliest mention and the making are one year

questions.explanation: A terminus post quem marks the point after which the work must have been made, so earlier dates are excluded and later ones remain possible. It is a floor, not a year of completion.
questions.hint: Ask what the term rules out.

options.misconception: asserts a rule instead of describing the usual relation

options.misconception: invents a botanical rule to explain the limitation

options.text: Reports are made only for panels that are already ruined.
options.misconception: claims reports exist only for ruined objects

options.text: It dates the timber, and the chart may have been painted on it much later.

questions.explanation: A tree-ring report dates the timber, and the gap between felling and painting may be long, so it gives a floor rather than a year. Botanical rules do not explain that limit.

questions.learningObjective: Judge what several clues together can establish.
questions.stem: Four findings are listed in the sheet as candidates for dating a chart. Which reading is correct?

options.text: A weave match and a pigment floor together prove the chart is a copy.
options.misconception: turns two constraints into a claim that the sheet is a copy

A pigment floor and a signed date together fix the year of the chart.
options.misconception: treats a floor and a signature as a single exact year

options.text: Neither clue is worth recording, since neither names an artist.
options.misconception: dismisses useful constraints because they name no artist

questions.explanation: Each finding constrains a different part of the story, the canvas and the date of the paint, so together they narrow the possibilities. Neither proves copying, fixes a year, or deserves dismissal.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An underdrawing read against the paint
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two layers should be read together.
questions.stem: Two survey readers are asked to explain how a drawing layer and the finished chart should be read together.

answer.exemplar: The drawing and the paint record two decisions at two moments, and the interest lies in the distance between them. Where the lines run on into the paint, the plan was kept; where they stop short of it, the plan was abandoned; where a line is doubled, a correction was made. Read together, the two layers give the sequence of the work in a way that neither gives alone, and a catalogue can then describe the chart as made rather than merely as it appears.

questions.explanation: Read together, the two layers show which parts of the plan were kept, changed or abandoned, which gives the sequence of the work. Read alone, the drawing suggests a chart that was never painted.
questions.hint: Ask what the distance between the layers shows.

The pigment analysis is wrong, since green was used on charts long before.
options.misconception: dismisses a laboratory result without contrary evidence

questions.explanation: A pigment first made in 1795 cannot be in paint applied earlier, so the chart and the atlas dating cannot both stand unchanged. The result does not say in which year the sheet was painted.

options.misconception: turns a floor into a ceiling as well

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An underdrawing read against the paint
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a buried drawing adds to a chart.
questions.stem: One note asks what a second drawing beneath a painted chart adds that the paint alone cannot show, and to name one.

answer.exemplar: The paint shows the coast as the cartographer finally presented it, and on its own it hides every decision that came before. A second drawing beneath it, whether a compass rose ruled in the margin or a shoreline that was begun and abandoned, records the plan as it stood at one moment. That lets a reader see the shape of the first idea, the point at which it was changed, and the difference between the working method and the finished chart.

questions.explanation: The paint shows the finished coast and hides the earlier decisions, while the drawing records the plan at one moment. Together they reveal the first idea and the point at which it changed.
questions.hint: Ask what the buried drawing preserves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ring date that conflicts with a paint date
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a conflict of dates must be resolved.
questions.stem: A second question asks the projection team why a ring date that conflicts with a paint date must be settled, and to say why.

answer.exemplar: A ring date and a paint date that cannot both stand describe a contradiction, and something in the chain has to give. Either the wood was reused long after it was cut, in which case the ring date is a limit and not a date; or the paint was applied to a panel that does not belong to the chart; or one of the analyses has been read wrongly. Each possibility has to be tested, because the choice between them changes the date assigned to the work.

questions.explanation: A conflict means the evidence cannot all stand as read, so the possibilities must be tested: reuse of old wood, a mismatch of panel and chart, or a misread analysis. The choice changes the date.
questions.hint: Ask what could explain the two dates.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an underdrawing should be read against the paint.
questions.stem: A note asks the editors to explain how an underdrawing should be read against the paint and what to look for.

answer.exemplar: The underdrawing should be read as a set of decisions still open. Where a drawn line runs into the painted area, the plan was kept; where it stops, the plan was given up; where a form is drawn twice, a correction was made; and where a ruled line crosses the finished coast, the sheet was planned on a grid. Setting the drawing against the paint in this way turns the two layers into a record of how the chart was made, not simply of how it looks.

questions.explanation: The drawing marks decisions still open, so comparing it with the paint shows what was kept, changed or abandoned. That turns two layers into a record of how the chart was made.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ring date that conflicts with a paint date
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a set of dates can stand together.

stimulus.body: A sheet annotation records that a chart's panel gives a felling date of 1622. Its paper is a laid paper first recorded in mills in 1630, and the sheet carries an inscription added in 1655.

questions.stem: A sheet thread places a report written in sixteen twenty-two beside later evidence. What does the evidence show?

options.text: A conflict, because the inscription must be the date of the painting.
options.misconception: treats a later inscription as if it fixed the painting date

options.text: A conflict, because the paper cannot be older than the panel.
options.misconception: invents a conflict between materials that are not rivals

options.text: A sequence of dates that the sheet can accommodate without any conflict.
That the panel must have been replaced, since the dates do not match.
options.misconception: jumps to a replacement to solve a difference in dates

questions.explanation: The wood, the paper and the inscription form an ordered sequence the sheet can accommodate, so no conflict arises. Reading the inscription as the painting date misreads the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the three dates can stand together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A panel made from older boards
questions.learningObjective: State what old boards in a panel tell the team.
questions.stem: A final annotation asks the editors first to state what old boards in a panel tell us and then to choose the option that fits.

options.text: That the chart was painted by a carpenter rather than a draughtsman.
options.misconception: infers the painter's trade from the reuse of boards

options.text: That the work was painted in the year the boards were cut.
options.misconception: makes the cutting of the wood the painting of the sheet

options.text: That the panel is older than the atlas it was later bound into.
options.misconception: compares the panel with the binding without a reason

options.text: That the work cannot be earlier than the boards were cut, and may be much later.

questions.explanation: Old boards set a floor for the work and may also signal a long interval before it was painted. They say nothing about the year, the binding or who did the painting.
questions.hint: Ask whether the wood fixes or limits the date.
